e.t: This Hebrew word means “Bethlehemite,” identifying someone from Bethlehem. It functions as a descriptive designation for a person, marking that person’s connection with the town rather than describing an action, object, or quality. In its eight Hebrew Old Testament occurrences, it appears in 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel and consistently refers to people associated with Bethlehem. Its precise role in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to mulberry trees. It is used as the name of a kind of tree, rather than as an action, quality, or person. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, in two historical accounts from 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. The word appears within spoken instructions, while the precise significance of each passage depends on its surrounding verse context.

This Hebrew word refers to “Baal,” functioning as a proper name rather than a general description. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both occurrences being in 2 Samuel 13:23. The associated rendering identifies the name as “Baal,” while the full Hebrew lemma is connected with Baal-hazor. Since the verse text is not included here, the word’s specific role in that passage cannot be described beyond its name reference.

e.t: Baanah is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It appears as the name of individuals in the Old Testament, including occurrences in Samuel, Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning in a particular passage comes from the person identified and the surrounding context, not from a general dictionary sense.

This Hebrew word means “defence,” functioning as a noun for something regarded as a place or means of protection. Its exact force in a sentence is shaped by the surrounding wording, but its central idea is protective security. It occurs only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, and both occurrences are in Job 22:24–25. Because no broader usage is recorded, this passage provides the word’s entire biblical Hebrew range in the available text.

Adamah is the Hebrew name rendered “Adamah.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 19:36, and no broader range of uses is represented here. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical item itself identifies “Adamah.”

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “pool,” referring to a collected body of water. It is used for pools as recognizable places within the Old Testament, including settings connected with travel, royal activity, building works, and the disposal of bodies. The word occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, across 15 verses. Its ordinary sense remains a physical pool or reservoir, while the surrounding verse determines what particular pool is being mentioned.

The word refers to “whelps,” functioning as a plural noun for young animals. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only twice, once in Jeremiah 51:38 and once in Nahum 2:12. Both occurrences have the same English rendering, so the basic lexical sense is consistent across this small Hebrew usage. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, not on the word alone.

This Hebrew noun means “fold,” naming a place where sheep are gathered or kept. It functions as a noun rather than describing an action or quality. The word appears three times in the Old Testament, in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Micah. Its basic sense remains focused on a fold as a defined place of gathering. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular force of the word in each occurrence.

This Hebrew word refers to a specific thing mentioned in Isaiah 30:6, but its precise meaning cannot be stated reliably from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, making it a rare term rather than a word whose normal use can be compared across many passages. The verse reference identifies where it occurs, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its particular sense there. Its lexical identity is preserved, but no English gloss or definition is available.

This Hebrew word refers to a falcon, a bird named in the Old Testament. It occurs only twice in the Hebrew Bible, once in Deuteronomy and once in Isaiah, so its meaning is specific rather than a broad description of birds generally. In both references, it identifies a particular bird within lists or descriptions of creatures. The word’s precise significance in either passage comes from the surrounding verse and its place among the other creatures mentioned.

This Hebrew word describes something as “fat.” It functions as a descriptive word, identifying a person, animal, or thing by that quality when used in a sentence. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament: twice in Psalms and once in Isaiah. The surrounding verse determines what is being described, but the basic lexical sense is simply “fat” here.

This Hebrew verb means “abhors,” describing a subject’s action toward something or someone. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 33:20. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its lexical contribution is the action expressed by “abhors,” directed toward an object.

This Hebrew word means “breast,” naming a body part. It is a noun used for the breast itself rather than an action or quality. It identifies this bodily part when it is mentioned in a sentence. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:32. Its basic lexical sense is “breast,” while the surrounding verse supplies the specific role and significance it has in that one occurrence.

This Hebrew word describes someone as “sick,” expressing a condition of physical weakness or illness. It functions as a verb, indicating that a person has become or is being sick rather than naming the person or condition itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 75 times, with this sense appearing repeatedly in accounts of people whose health has failed. Its broad use includes both brief statements about sickness and descriptions of serious physical decline.

This Hebrew word means “delight.” It expresses a person’s favorable inclination toward someone or something—what that person takes satisfaction in, wants, or is pleased to pursue. In a sentence, it commonly functions as the action or attitude of delighting, whether the subject is God, a ruler, or another person. It occurs 75 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a broad use for describing what someone gladly approves or desires. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “fillets,” a specific kind of band or decorative strip used in the tabernacle’s construction. It names a physical feature of the sanctuary furnishings rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Exodus, where it is associated with the tabernacle’s court and its completed furnishings. Its precise placement is determined by the surrounding construction instructions and descriptions.

This Hebrew word functions as a personal name, rendered “Ibneiah,” rather than as a general description or action. It identifies one individual in the Old Testament and appears once, in 1 Chronicles 9:8. Because it is used as a name, its ordinary role is to identify the person connected with that occurrence, not to express a quality, command, or event. The available rendering preserves the name “Ibneiah,” while the word’s broader meaning cannot be determined from this single naming use.

Joelah is a Hebrew personal name, functioning as the name of an individual rather than as a general description or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 12:7, and the English rendering preserves it as “Joelah.” No descriptive meaning is given for the name itself, so its clear lexical role is to identify that person. Its significance beyond this personal designation cannot be established from the available information.

e.t: Jotham is a personal name, referring to a man named Jotham rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is consistently rendered “Jotham” and occurs 24 times across 24 verses. The name appears in accounts involving people from Israel and Judah, including references in Judges, Kings, Chronicles, Isaiah, and Micah. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding account, but the word itself functions as a person’s name.

This Hebrew word functions as a verb meaning “be,” indicating that someone or something exists or is in a stated condition. It appears eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its role is normally understood from the sentence in which it occurs. The word is used in passages from Genesis through Ezekiel, including sentences describing people or things as being in a particular state. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and context.

Chiun is a name used as a specific designation rather than a general description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Amos 5:26, so its meaning is tied to identifying this particular named referent. The available wording preserves it as “Chiun,” rather than providing a broader descriptive definition. Its precise significance in Amos depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a proper name within that occurrence.

This Hebrew word means “yearned,” describing a strong inward longing. It presents yearning as an intense response arising within someone, rather than a simple outward action. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, including passages involving deep personal feeling and compassion. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a powerful inward yearning. The word appears in Genesis, 1 Kings, Lamentations, and Hosea.

In its 18 Old Testament occurrences, it appears mainly in descriptions of the lampstand and its construction in Exodus, where several such objects are incorporated into the design. It also occurs once each in Amos and Zephaniah. The precise force in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding wording.

Its use is consistently connected with the naming or condemnation of witchcraft rather than with an ordinary skill or harmless activity.

e.t: Ishod is a personal name, referring to a man named “Ishod” in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is not supplied with a separate lexical definition, so its ordinary meaning is the person’s name rather than an explained character quality or action. The name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:18, within a genealogical setting connected with birth or begetting. Its precise significance as a name is not stated.

e.t: “Libnites” is a group name for a family or clan recorded among the Israelites. It functions as a proper designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Numbers, where it appears in genealogical or census-related lists. Thus, the word identifies a particular people group within Israel’s family records, while the surrounding passage supplies the details of their place and ancestry.

This Hebrew word refers to a “piercing”—something that pierces or wounds. It functions as a noun describing the act or result of piercing rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 12:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and comparison, but the central idea remains a piercing injury or wound. The related English rendering is “piercing.”

This Hebrew noun means “compass,” referring to a tool used for drawing or marking a circle. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 44:13. Its basic sense is the instrument itself, rather than an action or quality. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its full role in that passage, but the word’s ordinary meaning is a compass used as a practical tool.

This Hebrew word refers to “dark,” describing a condition in which light is absent or obscured. It functions as a noun, naming darkness as a surrounding condition rather than describing an action. In the Old Testament, it occurs seven times, especially in the Psalms and Isaiah. Its uses can describe people being placed in or surrounded by darkness, including the imagery associated with a path that God makes known. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding wording.

This Hebrew word means “these,” referring to particular people or things that have already been identified or are being pointed out. It functions as a demonstrative expression, directing attention to specific items rather than describing a general group. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Jeremiah 10:11. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its exact emphasis in that sentence cannot be explained further; however, its basic sense is a pointing word that identifies the things under discussion.

This Hebrew word means “burning.” It refers to a burning condition discussed in the Old Testament’s examination of skin conditions. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Bible, all within Leviticus 13, and is rendered with the idea of burning in each occurrence. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a burning condition identified during the priestly examination described in that chapter.

Molech is the name of a pagan deity worshiped by some people in ancient Israel. In the Old Testament, the word functions as a proper name rather than a general description. It appears nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Leviticus, where the Lord forbids giving children to Molech. Other passages connect Molech with worship practices opposed to the Lord, showing that the name identifies an object of false worship and forbidden devotion. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Hammoleketh.” It is a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only once, in 1 Chronicles 7:18, within a genealogical record. The available biblical indexing places it as an object connected with birth or begetting, so its role there is to identify a person named in that family line.

Miphkad is a named Hebrew term rendered “Miphkad.” It functions as a proper name rather than a common descriptive word, so its ordinary meaning here is the identification of a particular named entity. In the Hebrew Bible corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 3:31. Because no verse text or explicit definition is available, the name itself is the clearest supported explanation; its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to fat or fatness, and can describe richness, abundance, or the well-being associated with fertile provision. It appears seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament. In some passages it describes the fatness of land or people; in others, it is something given or possessed. The related idea is fullness rather than thinness or lack, though the exact force depends on the sentence in which it appears. English translations commonly render it as “fat” or “fatness.”

This Hebrew verb means “slumber,” describing sleep or a state of being asleep. It is used of people who sleep and, in poetic passages, of those who fail to remain watchful. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Psalms, Isaiah, and Nahum. Its central idea remains simple: entering or remaining in sleep, whether considered naturally or as a failure to stay alert.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “spicery,” functioning as a noun that names a substance or trade good. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Genesis, so its recorded use is narrow rather than broad. The word appears in passages where it is treated as an object, but the available information does not include the verse text needed to describe its precise role in either setting. Its central meaning remains “spicery.”

Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its normal function is simply to name this individual.

e.t: Ebed is a Hebrew personal name. In the Old Testament, it identifies a particular man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears six times in six verses: five times in Judges 9 and once in Ezra 8. Its occurrences also appear in passages containing speech about or involving Ebed, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each specific scene. The English Bible renderings consistently preserve it as “Ebed.”

Adullam is the name of a place in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper place-name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in eight verses, and is consistently rendered “Adullam.” Because it identifies a location, its particular significance comes from the surrounding passage where the name occurs, rather than from a broader abstract meaning.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Amittai.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus: once in 2 Kings 14:25 and once in Jonah 1:1. In both recorded occurrences, English renderings preserve it as “Amittai,” confirming its function as a personal name. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical role is simply a person’s name.

This Hebrew word means “speak.” It expresses the action of speaking, functioning as the word that states what someone does rather than naming a person, place, or thing. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 50:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is the act of speaking or communicating through words.

This Hebrew word identifies a place named “Addar” or “Ataroth.” It functions as a proper name rather than a description of an action, quality, or person. The name occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, all in Joshua, where it appears in descriptions of territorial boundaries. The two approved English renderings preserve the same place-name while reflecting a spelling variation in translation.

This word refers to Ezion Geber, a place-name rather than a general object, action, or quality. It identifies a location mentioned in Israel’s journey history and in accounts of royal activity. The name appears 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across seven verses, and is rendered “Ezion” and “Geber.” Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding account, but its basic function is to identify this place.

This Hebrew word means “abundance,” expressing a plentiful supply or rich provision. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Jeremiah 33:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea is that something is present in generous measure rather than scarcity. The word therefore points to fullness and ample provision, while the surrounding context determines what is abundant.

פִּי־בֶסֶת is a Hebrew proper name, referring to a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in Ezekiel 30:17. The available material does not provide an English gloss or enough verse text to explain the name’s literal parts or its significance in that passage. Its exact role must therefore be understood from Ezekiel 30:17 and its surrounding context.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “graven” and functions as a noun for something made by carving. In the Old Testament, it appears in 24 verses and is commonly associated with objects set up or treated in worship. Its normal sense points to a carved representation rather than the living God. It occurs throughout the Old Testament, from Deuteronomy through Micah, with its precise force determined by the surrounding passage.

Zeboim is a proper place name, rendered “Zeboim” in English. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in 1 Samuel 13:18 and once in Nehemiah 11:34. Because it functions as a name rather than an ordinary descriptive word, its meaning is chiefly its identification of a particular place. The available references do not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the location or significance further. Its precise role in either passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “thorns,” referring to sharp growths that can wound, hinder, or make a path difficult. It occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, appearing once in Job and once in Proverbs. In Proverbs, it functions as the object associated with something from which a person must be kept or turned away. Its ordinary sense remains concrete: thorny growth that creates danger or obstruction. The surrounding verse determines how that image is applied in context.

The word occurs 43 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages concerning marital suspicion, devotion, and God’s response toward his people. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “charger,” naming a tangible object used among the furnishings and presented items described in Exodus and Numbers. It functions as the object being made, handled, or given, rather than as an action or quality. The word occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Numbers, where repeated offerings include this item. Its use in these passages consistently points to a physical vessel associated with worship and service.

This Hebrew word expresses being “called.” It is used when a person, place, or thing receives a designation, and it can function as the action of calling someone or something. The word appears 739 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that this is a broad and regularly used term rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on who is doing the calling and what or whom is being called.

e.t: This word means “thousand,” expressing a large counted quantity. It is used with numbers or groups to indicate how many people, objects, or units are being counted, rather than describing a quality or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 10 verses. Its use includes counted gifts and totals, showing its ordinary role as a numerical amount in a sentence.

This Hebrew word describes being high or elevated, and it can also express haughtiness or proud self-exaltation. Its meaning may refer to physical height, but in several passages it describes an attitude that places a person above others. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Proverbs, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its use in Isaiah connects human haughtiness with being brought low, showing the contrast between proud elevation and humble lowering. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is physical height or prideful exaltation.

This Hebrew word means “washing,” referring to the act or process of being washed. It functions as a noun naming that washing, rather than describing the person who performs it. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Song of Songs: 4:2 and 6:6. Its repeated use in these passages supports the same basic meaning, while the surrounding verse determines the specific image being described.

This Hebrew word expresses letting go, releasing, or becoming weak.
